Title: Instructional and institutional reforms necessary in health education in East Africa​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
NewsSummary: ​The need to transform health professionals’ education in order to strengthen health systems was the focus of a three day conference held at Safari Park Hotel.
NewsContent:
​The need to transform health professionals’ education in order to strengthen health systems was the focus of a three day conference held at Safari Park Hotel. This was organised by the Ea​stern Africa Health Professions Educators’ Association (EAHPEA) in partnership with Aga Khan University (AKU) and Anglia Ruskin University (UK).​

Participants were drawn from public and private institutions involved in health education in Kenya, Ug​​​anda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Ethiopia and Somalia. These included universities, medical training institutions and nursing schools. Over 10 professionals attended the forum.

The Conference used the framework of the 2010 Lancet Commission:  Health Professionals for a New Century: Transforming Education to Strengthen Health Systems in an Interdependent World (also known as the Frenk Report).

The Commission set out to review the global status of post-secondary professional education in health especially in medicine, public health and nursing. The guiding principles were to adopt a global outlook, focus on the health needs of the populations, recognise the increasing demand for integrated health professionals’ education and leadership and take a systems approach to education reform.

The Conference was centred on the implications of this Commission’s finding for East Africa. The problems discussed included the mismatch of competencies to patient and population needs, poor teamwork, weak leadership to improve health systems performance and hospital dominance over primary care.

The participants also dwelt on the need to invest more resources in the education of health professionals. The Frenk Report has pointed out that globally there was serious underfunding and underestimation of the need to train health professions and only less than two per cent of the available resources are allocated to their education. Substantial expansion of investments in health professional education is necessary from all sources: public, private, development aid and foundations.

Curriculum reform is a priority as what is used in most public health education centres in East Africa has not been reviewed regularly to keep up with the health implications of the 21st century. As a result students are not developing skills to make them competent in modern health care settings.

Also deliberated was interdependence and shared knowledge and the fact that harnessing of knowledge should not be restricted to a specific cadre of health-care providers. The traditional approach of learning in ‘silos’ does not favour collaborative practice which is a requirement once students graduate, as the workplace environment necessitates collaboration between nurses, doctors, pharmacists, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and other health care cadres for successful service delivery. The curriculum should be designed to give students exposure to primary, secondary and tertiary health care settings as well as enable them learn alongside their colleagues in different health-care professions. Instructional designs of learning should embrace the use of Information Technology (IT), is a powerful tool in education as this creates the potential for easy retrieval of information for evidence-based practice, a requirement for successful life-long learners.

Leadership on reform issues has to come from within the academic and professional communities, but it must be backed by political leaders in government and society. The discussions placed emphasis on trans-professional education especially training non-professional health workers and community leaders so that they can develop competencies and cascade the right messages to the local people.

A highlight of the Conference was the official launch of the East Africa Health Professions Ed​ucators’ Association (EAHPEA). Among those who attended the launch were Professor David Serwadda, the East Africa Commissioner on the Frenk Report,  Professor Sarah Kiguli of Makerere University Chair of EAHPEA, Professor Robert Armstrong, the Foundation Dean of the Medical College at Aga Khan University, Professor Yasmin Amarsi, Dean of the Aga Khan University School of Nursing, Professor Patrick Kyamanywa, Dean of the National University of Rwanda Medical College and Professor Charles Mkony of  School of Medicine, Muhimbili University of Health & Allied Sciences, Tanzania. A panel of distinguished guests, Chaired by Professor Barasa Kwa- Otsyula, head of the Education Committee of the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists’ Board,  discussed the emerging transformations in health professional education including the balance between service and training, retention of practioners in public service, modernising information systems and the setting of service standards for health care delivery. The panel included, Dr Joseph Cosam, CEO of the Inter-university Council for East Africa, Mr Daniel Yumbya, CEO of the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists’ Board, Dr Kefa Bosire of the University of Nairobi’s Medical Education Programme Initiative, Ms Milly Kabanga, Director of Mulago Health tutor’s college in Uganda, and Professor Stephen Okeyo of FUNZO Kenya Project.

​Prof. Sarah Kiguli explained that the EAHPEA has grown out of the expressed needs of health professions’ educa​tors working to deliver service to today's patients whilst training tomorrow’s professionals.  Greater educational knowledge and skills enable them to bec​ome more effective in both domains and improve the health care of their patients.  It is from this foundation that the association has grown and developed.

She said, “Our objective is to promote inter-professional collaboration between healt​​h professionals, that is, nurses, pharmacists, medical doctors, dentists and other allied ​health care providers and in particularly foster team work among them. We also aim to encourage dialogue and corporation among East Africa’s researchers and specia​lists in the​ field of health education.”
